summary.text: A weather satellite is an Earth observation satellite used mainly to monitor the Earth's weather and climate.
They come mainly in two types: polar orbiting ones that cover the whole Earth, and geostationary ones that hover over one spot on the equator.
Besides tracking storms and clouds, they detect fires, pollution, dust storms and snow cover, and together give nearly continuous global observations.

paragraphs.heading: Eyes on the weather
paragraphs.text: A weather satellite is a kind of Earth observation satellite whose main job is watching Earth's weather and climate. Most are one of two types. Polar orbiting satellites cover the entire Earth, while geostationary satellites stay over the same spot on the equator.

paragraphs.heading: More than clouds
paragraphs.text: Their main use is spotting how storms and cloud patterns form and move, but they also pick up city lights, fires, pollution, auroras, dust storms, snow cover and the edges of ocean currents. Satellite images helped track the ash cloud from Mount St. Helens. El Niño is watched daily through them, and the Antarctic ozone hole is mapped from their data. Together, satellites flown by the US, China, Europe, India, Russia and Japan give nearly continuous observations for a global weather watch.

paragraphs.heading: A shaky start
paragraphs.text: The idea of cameras in orbit to watch the weather was already being developed in 1946, because observations were sparse and cloud cameras on rockets were costly. The first weather satellite, Vanguard 2, went up on February 17, 1959. A poor axis of rotation and its elliptical orbit meant it gathered little useful data. The first one counted as a success was NASA's TIROS-1, launched on April 1, 1960, which worked for 78 days.

paragraphs.heading: Better forecasts from orbit
paragraphs.text: TIROS led to the Nimbus program, whose technology lies behind most Earth-observing satellites that NASA and NOAA have launched since. Starting with Nimbus 3 in 1969, satellites retrieved temperatures through the troposphere over the eastern Atlantic and most of the Pacific, which greatly improved forecasts. Geostationary satellites followed, first the ATS and SMS series and then GOES from the 1970s. Polar orbiters such as QuikScat and TRMM later reported winds near the ocean surface, which greatly improved judging the strength and location of tropical cyclones in the 2000s and 2010s.

paragraphs.heading: Europe's Meteosat
paragraphs.text: Europe launched its first geostationary weather satellite, Meteosat-1, in 1977. A series followed up to Meteosat-7, which gathered data from 1997 until 2017, run first by the European Space Agency and later by EUMETSAT. The third generation began with Meteosat-12 in 2022. Its imager satellites scan the full Earth disc every ten minutes and carry a new Lightning Imager.

paragraphs.heading: Watching space weather
paragraphs.text: NOAA's DSCOVR, launched in 2015, became the first deep space satellite able to observe and predict space weather. It can detect hazards such as the solar wind and geomagnetic storms. That ability has allowed accurate space weather forecasts made ahead of time since the late 2010s.
